readings.title: The ramp behind the building
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A civic centre had a step-free entrance, yet visitors using wheelchairs often arrived at the front steps and had to turn back. The main obstacle was an accessible route hidden from the street. The ramp was at the rear, and the first directional sign appeared only after the main doorway. At first, the people involved did not agree on which part of the proposal deserved the most attention.

To investigate, the team used a visitor route walk-through. The team asked people with different mobility needs to approach from the bus stop and describe each decision point. The organizers kept the first stage small enough to change without wasting substantial time or resources.

The evidence indicated the problem began before visitors reached the door. The physical ramp worked, but people could not locate it from the place where their journey began. The group then introduced signs placed at the earliest route choices. Staff also updated maps and made sure the rear entrance was open whenever the building was in use. The records were useful because they described ordinary use rather than an ideal situation imagined at a meeting.

The case suggests a broader point: accessibility begins with finding the route. A useful facility cannot meet its purpose if visitors discover it only after facing a barrier. The group published its reasons so that people who preferred a different result could still understand the choice. For those taking part in the ramp behind the building, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records.

readings.title: A quieter hour at a museum
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A local museum offered a quiet visiting hour. Families welcomed the idea, but the experience remained noisy in one gallery. The main obstacle was sound from an automatic video display. The announcement promised reduced noise without identifying a screen that played loudly whenever visitors entered. The question mattered to people with different schedules and levels of experience, so one account could not represent everyone.

To investigate, the team used observations made during two trial visits. Staff recorded sound sources and invited visitors to say which parts of the route were difficult. A simple record of what happened each day gave the team a starting point for comparison.

The evidence indicated one predictable sound caused most concern. The number of people in the gallery was less important than the video that could not be anticipated. The group then introduced captions with the video sound turned off. The museum offered a clear description of the quieter route and kept other hours unchanged. Some participants welcomed the change immediately, while others noticed practical details that needed further work.

The case suggests a broader point: inclusive arrangements require specific checks. A label such as quiet is meaningful only when the full visitor experience matches it. The result was a revised plan, not a claim that every difficulty had disappeared. For those taking part in a quieter hour at a museum, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: Reading a public notice outdoors
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A council placed information beside a riverside path. Many walkers stopped but left without understanding a map of temporary closures. The main obstacle was a map too small to read from the path. The notice was mounted behind bright glass and relied on colours that looked similar in sunlight. The initial idea sounded reasonable, yet the details of the place made it harder to carry out than expected.

To investigate, the team used a practical reading exercise on site. Designers watched people try to identify the closed section from normal standing positions. Instead of relying on a single opinion, the team invited several users to describe what they actually did.

The evidence indicated large words and landmarks worked better than colours. Visitors could follow a plain sentence naming the bridge and path entrance even when the map remained difficult. The group then introduced a larger text notice with a simplified map. The council named the alternative route in words and checked the sign under daytime conditions. This allowed the organizers to separate a temporary inconvenience from a pattern that required attention.

The case suggests a broader point: information must work where it is used. A notice that looks clear on a computer may fail beside a sunny, busy walkway. They also decided when to check the arrangement again, because conditions could change over time. For those taking part in reading a public notice outdoors, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

readings.title: A community meeting with captions
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
Residents watched a streamed planning meeting. People with hearing difficulties said the live captions sometimes missed speakers names. The main obstacle was unclear attribution in the meeting record. When several speakers answered quickly, viewers could not tell who supported each proposal. The people affected were invited to comment before a permanent arrangement was chosen.

To investigate, the team used a review with caption users. Organizers compared the recording with the caption text and asked viewers where meaning had been lost. The first trial produced both useful results and questions the team could not yet answer.

The evidence indicated speaker labels were as important as word accuracy. Correct sentences still confused readers when they appeared without a clear link to the person speaking. The group then introduced microphone rules and corrected posted captions. The chair asked each speaker to identify themselves and published a checked transcript afterward. Rather than hide those limits, the public note explained how the next version had been selected.

The case suggests a broader point: accessible communication includes context. People need to know not only what was said, but also who said it and when. That explanation made later changes easier to discuss with residents and staff. For those taking part in a community meeting with captions, the value of the work lay in connecting a specific observation to a visible decision. People could question the result because the process had been explained. No single trial could settle every issue. The group planned to keep listening after the new arrangement began and to compare later experiences with its first records. This gradual approach allowed the organizers to protect the original aim while changing a method that had not worked as expected in everyday use.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
When a community changes the public access improvement programme, a short explanation can be as important as the change itself. People want to know what problem was noticed, how information was gathered and why one option was selected. For a project about accessibility and public space, staff observed actual use rather than relying only on a drawing or an early promise. The evidence revealed an obstacle that was not obvious at first. Organizers made a limited adjustment and told residents when it would be reviewed. They also described the limits of the trial, because a small number of visits cannot represent every future situation. An honest account made the decision easier to question and improve.

translation.referenceAnswer: 社区调整一项服务时，简短解释可能和改动本身同样重要。人们想知道发现了什么问题、如何收集信息，以及为何选择某个方案。在一个有关无障碍与公共空间的项目中，工作人员观察实际使用，而不只依靠图纸或最初的承诺。证据揭示了起初并不明显的障碍。组织者作出有限调整，并告知居民何时重新评估。他们也说明试行的局限，因为少量使用经历不能代表未来所有情况。诚实的说明让这项决定更容易被讨论和改进。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to the accessibility working group suggesting a practical change to the public access improvement programme. Describe who should be consulted, how the change could be tried, and when it should be reviewed.
writing.explanation: 范文供考生自评，注意任务要点、组织结构及语言准确性。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Committee Members,
I would like to propose a small improvement to the public access improvement programme. People have noticed an accessible route hidden from the street, and a short trial could help us understand how often this problem occurs. We should ask regular users and people who have not used the service before to describe their experiences. Their comments may reveal details that a plan made in an office would miss.
For one month, staff could keep a simple record of participation, time spent and any difficulties reported. We should also explain the purpose of the trial in clear language so that residents know how to contribute. After the month, please publish a brief summary of both benefits and limits. The final decision should be based on what people actually experienced, with a date for checking the arrangement again.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
